screens.title: What is cross-chaincode invocation?
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-chaincode invocation is the mechanism that lets one chaincode call a function inside another chaincode as part of the same transaction. The purpose is straightforward: keep contracts focused. For example, an Asset chaincode can manage ownership while an Audit chaincode records events. When Asset performs a transfer, it calls the Audit chaincode to persist an audit entry. This keeps audit logic reusable and separate. A common misconception is that the called chaincode runs in a separate transaction; it does not. Invocations occur within the same transaction context, and Fabric guarantees atomicity across the involved states. That means if any invoked chaincode returns an error, the whole transaction is rolled back. Another misconception is that you can pass plain strings as args; in Fabric you must pass a slice of byte arrays where the first element is the target function name. A practical analogy: think of chaincodes as small services in the same process that can call each other; they share the transaction but enforce their own endorsement policies. Consider this when you design responsibilities so that sensitive data stays isolated yet accessible where needed. How might you split responsibilities in your current dApp to gain reuse without introducing tight coupling?

keyIdea.text: Cross-chaincode invocation composes specialized chaincodes into a single atomic transaction, enabling modular orchestration.

content.html:
Core Concept
Cross-chaincode invocation
Invoke one chaincode from another to separate concerns and reuse functionality.
Quick bullets
  • Calls happen inside the same transaction context and are atomic.
  • Args must be a [][]byte slice; first element is function name.
  • Empty channel string means same-channel invocation.
  • Endorsement policies of all involved chaincodes must be satisfied.
Key Takeaway

Treat cross-chaincode invocation as inter-contract calls inside a single transaction that preserve atomicity and require proper endorsement planning.

Analogy & Example
Analogy
Think of chaincodes as focused services. One service writes an order; another records an audit. Both run in the same orchestrated transaction.
Concrete
Asset chaincode invokes audit_log with args: function name followed by event details, then checks response.Status for success.
Common misconception
Invoked chaincode does not execute in a separate commit. It participates in the same transaction, so design for rollback semantics and endorsement unions.

screens.title: Using stub.InvokeChaincode
screens.narratorSegment: The essential call is stub. InvokeChaincode(chaincodeName, args, channel). ChaincodeName is the deployment name of the target contract. Args must be a slice of byte arrays where the first element is the function name and following elements are function parameters. If the target chaincode is on the same channel, pass an empty string for the channel parameter. If the chaincode lives on another channel, pass that channel name. A frequent error is passing a []string or forgetting to encode arguments as bytes. Also check the response. Status after the call; a non-OK status means the invoked chaincode returned an error and you should handle that by returning an error yourself so Fabric rolls back the entire transaction. Remember that endorsement policies across all touched chaincodes must be satisfied. Below is a short, focused code fragment showing how to prepare args and invoke a called chaincode. Study the example and note how errors propagate back to the caller so the transaction can fail cleanly. Using stub.InvokeChaincode means prepare args as [][]byte, call invokechaincode with correct channel string, and always validate response.status to manage atomic failures.. In practical terms, signature, args format, and channel parameter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
API Reference
stub.InvokeChaincode(chaincodeName, args, channel)
Prepare arguments as a slice of byte arrays. First element: function name. Subsequent: parameters.
Checklist
  • Use [][]byte; do not pass []string.
  • Pass "" for same-channel calls.
  • Check response.Status and response.Message.
  • Plan endorsement policies across all chaincodes involved.
Pro tip

Deploy and register the called chaincode before invoking it so the name matches and calls succeed at runtime.

Code example (visual)
auditArgs := [][]byte{[]byte("RecordAuditEntry"), []byte("AssetCreated"), []byte(assetID), []byte(details)}
response := ctx.GetStub().InvokeChaincode("audit_log", auditArgs, "")
if response.Status != shim.OK {
  return fmt.Errorf("failed to invoke audit_log chaincode: %s", response.Message)
}
Notes
  • Marshal complex arguments before converting to []byte if necessary.
  • Handle negative responses by returning an error to trigger rollback.

keyIdea.title: Called chaincode pattern
keyIdea.text: Implement precise, composable functions that return clear errors and store state under predictable keys for querying.

content.html:
Definition
AuditEntry and RecordAuditEntry
The called chaincode builds an audit object and persists it with composite keys for querying.
type AuditEntry struct {
  TxID      string    `json:"txId"`
  Timestamp time.Time `json:"timestamp"`
  EventType string    `json:"eventType"`
  AssetID   string    `json:"assetId"`
  Details   string    `json:"details"`
}

func (s *AuditLogChaincode) RecordAuditEntry(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, eventType, assetID, details string) error {
  txID := ctx.GetStub().GetTxID()
  timestamp, err := ctx.GetStub().GetTxTimestamp()
  if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to get transaction timestamp: %v", err)
  }

  entry := AuditEntry{TxID: txID, Timestamp: time.Unix(timestamp.GetSeconds(), int64(timestamp.GetNanos())), EventType: eventType, AssetID: assetID, Details: details}
  entryBytes, err := json.Marshal(entry)
  if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal audit entry: %v", err)
  }

  compositeKey, err := ctx.GetStub().CreateCompositeKey("AuditEntryByAsset", []string{assetID, txID})
  if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to create composite key: %v", err)
  }
  return ctx.GetStub().PutState(compositeKey, entryBytes)
}
Why this matters
Composite keys enable efficient queries by asset. Clear error returns let caller decide whether to roll back.
Concrete example
asset_management creates asset A123 and invokes RecordAuditEntry("AssetCreated", "A123", "owner X, value 100") to record the event.
Check your understanding
What additional composite keys would you create to query by event type? How would that affect storage and queries?

keyIdea.title: Caller pattern
keyIdea.text: Write the caller to prepare args, invoke the called chaincode, check the response, and return errors to preserve atomic behavior.

content.html:
Process
CreateAsset → Persist → Invoke audit_log
Verify existence, put state, then call the audit chaincode and check its response to ensure atomic commit.
func (s *AssetManagementChaincode) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, assetID string, owner string, value int) error {
  exists, err := s.AssetExists(ctx, assetID)
  if err != nil { return err }
  if exists { return fmt.Errorf("the asset %s already exists", assetID) }

  asset := Asset{ID: assetID, Owner: owner, Value: value}
  assetBytes, _ := json.Marshal(asset)
  if err := ctx.GetStub().PutState(assetID, assetBytes); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to put asset to world state: %v", err)
  }

  auditArgs := [][]byte{[]byte("RecordAuditEntry"), []byte("AssetCreated"), []byte(assetID), []byte(fmt.Sprintf("New asset created with owner %s and value %d", owner, value))}
  response := ctx.GetStub().InvokeChaincode("audit_log", auditArgs, "")
  if response.Status != shim.OK {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to invoke audit_log chaincode: %s", response.Message)
  }
  return nil
}
Example scenario
Create asset A1 for owner Alice with value 100 triggers an audit entry recording 'AssetCreated' with details about owner and value.
Common mistake
Passing args as []string or omitting response.Status checks leads to silent failures or incorrect state that isn't rolled back.
Check your understanding
If audit_log returns an error, should the asset be persisted? Explain why the transaction should fail to keep state consistent.

screens.title: Same-channel vs Different-channel invocation
screens.narratorSegment: Invoking a chaincode on the same channel uses an empty string for the channel parameter. This makes the called chaincode visible to the same set of peers and participants already part of the channel. Use same-channel invocation when the functionality should be available to the same consortium members and when you want tight coupling with shared world state. Different-channel invocation requires specifying the target channel name. This isolates the called chaincode to another audience and can be used when sensitive data should be guarded by a more restrictive channel membership. A practical example: keep audit data on a restricted audit channel and call it from an application channel by specifying that channel name. Remember, different-channel calls still participate in transaction atomicity only when permitted by network configuration; endorsement and visibility rules become more complex. A common misconception is thinking channel arguments act like namespaces only; they also control membership, visibility, and which peers can endorse. When designing cross-channel calls, plan where data should reside and which organizations must endorse the combined transaction. Same-channel vs Different-channel invocation means empty string = same channel (shared visibility). named channel = isolated visibility and separate membership; plan accordingly for endorsement and access.. In practical terms, when to use an empty channel and when to specify a channel name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Empty string = same channel (shared visibility). Named channel = isolated visibility and separate membership; plan accordingly for endorsement and access.

content.html:
Comparison
Same Channel
Use an empty string for the channel parameter to invoke a chaincode deployed to the same channel.
Characteristics
  • Shared world state visibility among channel members.
  • Simpler access model when all participants are trusted for the action.
  • Typical for tightly coupled application components.
Different Channel
Provide the channel name to invoke a chaincode on another channel, isolating data and membership.
Characteristics
  • Restricts access to the target channel's members.
  • Useful for auditing, compliance, or sharing with limited participants.
  • Requires careful endorsement and visibility planning across channels.
Concrete call examples
ctx.GetStub().InvokeChaincode("audit_log", auditArgs, "")
ctx.GetStub().InvokeChaincode("audit_log", auditArgs, "audit-channel")

screens.title: Atomicity and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: A crucial property when invoking multiple chaincodes is atomicity: Fabric treats the entire set of state changes as part of a single transaction. If any called chaincode returns an error, the peer will mark the transaction as invalid and no state changes across the involved chaincodes will be committed. This means the caller must always check response. Status and return an error upwards if the invoked chaincode failed. A common pitfall is ignoring response. Status and assuming eventual consistency; doing so can leave your application in an inconsistent state because peers will later reject or accept based on endorsement and validation. Another key point is endorsement policies: every chaincode touched by the transaction has its own policy, and the transaction only commits if the union of these policies is satisfied by the collected endorsements. Practical steps: validate inputs before invoking, check response. Status, log helpful messages for debugging, and design tests that simulate failure in called chaincodes to verify rollback behavior. A final question to reflect on: how will you design tests that simulate a failing called chaincode to ensure your caller handles rollbacks correctly?

keyIdea.title: Atomicity rule
keyIdea.text: If any part of a cross-chaincode transaction fails, Fabric rolls back all state changes; always check responses and propagate errors.

content.html:
Process Flow
Transaction lifecycle with cross-chaincode calls
1. Prepare & Validate
Validate inputs locally to avoid unnecessary state updates or calls.
2. Persist caller state
Optionally write state, but be consistent in ordering since all changes are part of the same transaction.
3. Invoke called chaincodes
Call InvokeChaincode and check response.Status for each invocation.
Failure handling
  • Return an error if any invoke returns non-OK to trigger a rollback.
  • Include context in error messages for debugging across chaincodes.
  • Write integration tests that simulate invoked chaincode failures to confirm rollback.
Common mistake

Assuming partial commits are acceptable. Fabric will accept or reject the whole transaction; design your logic with that all-or-nothing contract in mind.

screens.title: Design and dependency management
screens.narratorSegment: Good architecture keeps responsibilities clear and avoids circular dependencies. When designing multiple chaincodes, assign single responsibilities—identity, audit, inventory, orders—so each chaincode's A P I is narrow and well-tested. Avoid designs where Chaincode A calls B and B calls A back in the same transaction; such circular patterns can lead to confusion, complex endorsement requirements, and potential infinite loops. Instead, prefer one-way orchestrations or an orchestrator that composes calls deterministically. Also centralize common utilities in reusable chaincodes, for example a KYC or rewards contract, but be careful about endorsement policy aggregation: reusing a chaincode increases the number of required endorsements for a transaction, since the union of policies must be satisfied. Document the chaincode dependencies, choose names consistently during deployment, and include integration tests that validate failure modes. A practical step: create small test contracts that intentionally return errors so callers exercise rollback paths. How will you document and enforce the intended dependency graph for your deployed chaincodes? Design and dependency management means design one-way invocation flows, document dependencies, avoid circular calls, and plan endorsement policies for reused chaincodes.. In practical terms, patterns to avoid circular calls and unclear ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture
Design patterns for safe invocations
Single responsibility
Keep chaincodes focused: inventory, orders, audit, and KYC separated for clarity.
Avoid circular calls
Prefer linear orchestration or a dedicated orchestrator to prevent loops and complex policies.
Document dependencies
Maintain a dependency graph and deployment naming convention to avoid mismatches.

content.html:
Lab Overview
Terminal demo: deploy and run commands
Follow these high-level steps in your test network: implement inventory, implement orders, deploy inventory first, deploy orders, initialize inventory, then invoke PlaceOrder and QueryStock to observe results.
# Initialize inventory
peer chaincode invoke -C mychannel -n inventory_management -c '{"Args":["InitLedger"]}'

# Place order (successful)
peer chaincode invoke -C mychannel -n order_management -c '{"Args":["PlaceOrder","ORDER1","CUST1","PROD_A","2"]}'

# Query order and stock
peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n order_management -c '{"Args":["QueryOrder","ORDER1"]}'
peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n inventory_management -c '{"Args":["QueryStock","PROD_A"]}'

# Place order (insufficient stock)
peer chaincode invoke -C mychannel -n order_management -c '{"Args":["PlaceOrder","ORDER2","CUST2","PROD_B","999"]}'
Testing tips
Start with small quantities, test success then simulate failures, and inspect peer logs for error messages from invoked chaincodes.
Extension
Modify PlaceOrder to also invoke customer_rewards:UpdateCustomerPoints to understand endorsement policy unions when adding another called chaincode.
Why this lab matters
Running commands and seeing outputs helps you connect code-level patterns with runtime transaction behavior and rollback semantics.

screens.title: Pitfalls: naming, args, infinite loops, and system chaincodes
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson collects common mistakes and how to avoid them. First, chaincode naming mismatches are frequent: the name passed to InvokeChaincode must match the deployed name exactly. If it doesn't, the call fails. Second, argument formatting errors happen when developers pass []string or forget to convert parameters to []byte. Always prepare a [][]byte slice with the function name first. Third, infinite loops and circular invocations can cause runaway execution. Design one-way orchestrations or a clear orchestrator contract and avoid mutual calls within the same transaction. Fourth, error handling is essential: check response. Status and return meaningful errors so Fabric can roll back. Fifth, remember system chaincodes like cscc and _lifecycle can be invoked for management tasks but require special care and permissions. Lastly, endorsement policy union requirements mean adding reused chaincodes increases the set of endorsements required. Test policies in your staging environment to confirm commit behavior. By anticipating these pitfalls you can design more robust cross-chaincode interactions. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three essential concepts to carry forward. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why and how a chaincode calls another chaincode inside Hyperledger Fabric. Modularizing business logic into specialized chaincodes improves reuse, maintainability, and security. We will look at the core A P I that makes this possible and study a practical example where an asset management chaincode records events in an audit log chaincode. You will also learn the difference between invoking a chaincode on the same channel versus invoking one on a different channel, and the implications for access and endorsement. By the end, you'll understand common pitfalls such as argument formatting, naming mismatches, endorsement policy unions, and the risk of circular invocations. A small concrete scenario—placing an order that deducts inventory—will show how atomicity ensures that either all changes succeed or none are committed. Keep an eye out for the code examples; they demonstrate correct invocation patterns and error handling you can reuse. Consider how splitting responsibilities into separate chaincodes could make your own dApps easier to test and to secure.

These objectives map to the practical skills you'll gain. First, you'll understand why modular chaincodes matter: splitting logic into focused contracts reduces complexity and allows reuse. For example, you might keep identity checks in a KYC chaincode and asset operations in an Asset chaincode, then compose them via invocation. Second, you'll learn the exact signature and argument format for the InvokeChaincode A P I so you can call functions reliably. That includes preparing a [][]byte args slice with the function name first and remembering to pass an empty string for same-channel calls. Third, you'll learn to distinguish same-channel and different-channel invocations and how channel boundaries affect visibility and access. Finally, you'll learn to manage dependencies and data consistency: how to check response. Status, handle errors, and reason about atomic commits when multiple chaincodes participate. Each objective targets a practical competency you can verify by implementing the example chaincodes in the hands-on activity.

On this follow-up objectives slide we'll translate goals into concrete practice. You'll be able to write a calling chaincode that formats arguments as a [][]byte slice and invokes a target function reliably. For example, creating a new asset and then calling a separate audit_log chaincode to record the event shows how a single business transaction can compose specialized contracts. You'll also learn the testing and deployment steps: deploy the called chaincode first, confirm its name matches the invocation string, and run integration tests that validate atomic behavior when a called chaincode returns an error. Finally, you'll practice design choices: avoid circular invocations that can cause infinite loops and be mindful of endorsement policy unions so the transaction can commit. These outcomes prepare you for the hands-on lab where you'll implement order and inventory chaincodes and verify both success and failure flows.

Cross-chaincode invocation is the mechanism that lets one chaincode call a function inside another chaincode as part of the same transaction. The purpose is straightforward: keep contracts focused. For example, an Asset chaincode can manage ownership while an Audit chaincode records events. When Asset performs a transfer, it calls the Audit chaincode to persist an audit entry. This keeps audit logic reusable and separate. A common misconception is that the called chaincode runs in a separate transaction; it does not. Invocations occur within the same transaction context, and Fabric guarantees atomicity across the involved states. That means if any invoked chaincode returns an error, the whole transaction is rolled back. Another misconception is that you can pass plain strings as args; in Fabric you must pass a slice of byte arrays where the first element is the target function name. A practical analogy: think of chaincodes as small services in the same process that can call each other; they share the transaction but enforce their own endorsement policies. Consider this when you design responsibilities so that sensitive data stays isolated yet accessible where needed. How might you split responsibilities in your current dApp to gain reuse without introducing tight coupling?

The essential call is stub. InvokeChaincode(chaincodeName, args, channel). ChaincodeName is the deployment name of the target contract. Args must be a slice of byte arrays where the first element is the function name and following elements are function parameters. If the target chaincode is on the same channel, pass an empty string for the channel parameter. If the chaincode lives on another channel, pass that channel name. A frequent error is passing a []string or forgetting to encode arguments as bytes. Also check the response. Status after the call; a non-OK status means the invoked chaincode returned an error and you should handle that by returning an error yourself so Fabric rolls back the entire transaction. Remember that endorsement policies across all touched chaincodes must be satisfied. Below is a short, focused code fragment showing how to prepare args and invoke a called chaincode. Study the example and note how errors propagate back to the caller so the transaction can fail cleanly. Using stub.InvokeChaincode means prepare args as [][]byte, call invokechaincode with correct channel string, and always validate response.status to manage atomic failures.. In practical terms, signature, args format, and channel parameter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's examine the called chaincode that records audit entries. The audit_log chaincode defines an AuditEntry struct containing a transaction ID, timestamp, event type, asset ID, and details. The RecordAuditEntry function uses the transaction context to obtain the current transaction ID and timestamp, builds the entry, marshals it to JSON, then stores it under a composite key that includes the asset ID and tx ID. This design allows querying audit entries by asset. A concrete example: when asset_management creates an asset, it invokes RecordAuditEntry with eventType 'AssetCreated' and details describing the owner and value. A common error is failing to check for errors from GetTxTimestamp or JSON marshaling, so the example handles and returns those errors. Also note that PutState is used to persist the entry under a composite key. Remember: the called chaincode should return informative errors so the caller can react and ensure correct rollback semantics. How would you extend this design to index by event type as well? Audit Log chaincode (called) means implement precise, composable functions that return clear errors and store state under predictable keys for querying.. In practical terms, inspect recordauditentry implementation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now examine the calling chaincode that manages assets and invokes audit_log after creating or transferring assets. The CreateAsset function checks for existence, writes the asset to world state, then prepares auditArgs as a [][]byte slice with the RecordAuditEntry function name and the event details. It calls InvokeChaincode with an empty channel string for same-channel invocation and checks response. Status. If the called chaincode returns an error, CreateAsset returns an error to ensure Fabric rolls back the transaction. TransferAsset follows the same pattern: read state, update owner, persist the change, then invoke the audit_log with the transfer event. A frequent misunderstanding is to update state after invoking the called chaincode; doing so can still work, but be consistent and reason about the order since all changes participate in a single transaction. This code demonstrates safe error propagation and reuse of audit functionality without duplicating audit logic inside asset_management. Asset Management chaincode (caller) means write the caller to prepare args, invoke the called chaincode, check the response, and return errors to preserve atomic behavior.. In practical terms, create and transfer asset while invoking audit_log. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Invoking a chaincode on the same channel uses an empty string for the channel parameter. This makes the called chaincode visible to the same set of peers and participants already part of the channel. Use same-channel invocation when the functionality should be available to the same consortium members and when you want tight coupling with shared world state. Different-channel invocation requires specifying the target channel name. This isolates the called chaincode to another audience and can be used when sensitive data should be guarded by a more restrictive channel membership. A practical example: keep audit data on a restricted audit channel and call it from an application channel by specifying that channel name. Remember, different-channel calls still participate in transaction atomicity only when permitted by network configuration; endorsement and visibility rules become more complex. A common misconception is thinking channel arguments act like namespaces only; they also control membership, visibility, and which peers can endorse. When designing cross-channel calls, plan where data should reside and which organizations must endorse the combined transaction. Same-channel vs Different-channel invocation means empty string = same channel (shared visibility). named channel = isolated visibility and separate membership; plan accordingly for endorsement and access.. In practical terms, when to use an empty channel and when to specify a channel name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A crucial property when invoking multiple chaincodes is atomicity: Fabric treats the entire set of state changes as part of a single transaction. If any called chaincode returns an error, the peer will mark the transaction as invalid and no state changes across the involved chaincodes will be committed. This means the caller must always check response. Status and return an error upwards if the invoked chaincode failed. A common pitfall is ignoring response. Status and assuming eventual consistency; doing so can leave your application in an inconsistent state because peers will later reject or accept based on endorsement and validation. Another key point is endorsement policies: every chaincode touched by the transaction has its own policy, and the transaction only commits if the union of these policies is satisfied by the collected endorsements. Practical steps: validate inputs before invoking, check response. Status, log helpful messages for debugging, and design tests that simulate failure in called chaincodes to verify rollback behavior. A final question to reflect on: how will you design tests that simulate a failing called chaincode to ensure your caller handles rollbacks correctly?

Good architecture keeps responsibilities clear and avoids circular dependencies. When designing multiple chaincodes, assign single responsibilities—identity, audit, inventory, orders—so each chaincode's A P I is narrow and well-tested. Avoid designs where Chaincode A calls B and B calls A back in the same transaction; such circular patterns can lead to confusion, complex endorsement requirements, and potential infinite loops. Instead, prefer one-way orchestrations or an orchestrator that composes calls deterministically. Also centralize common utilities in reusable chaincodes, for example a KYC or rewards contract, but be careful about endorsement policy aggregation: reusing a chaincode increases the number of required endorsements for a transaction, since the union of policies must be satisfied. Document the chaincode dependencies, choose names consistently during deployment, and include integration tests that validate failure modes. A practical step: create small test contracts that intentionally return errors so callers exercise rollback paths. How will you document and enforce the intended dependency graph for your deployed chaincodes? Design and dependency management means design one-way invocation flows, document dependencies, avoid circular calls, and plan endorsement policies for reused chaincodes.. In practical terms, patterns to avoid circular calls and unclear ownership. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Always prepare a [][]byte slice with the function name first. Third, infinite loops and circular invocations can cause runaway execution. Design one-way orchestrations or a clear orchestrator contract and avoid mutual calls within the same transaction. Fourth, error handling is essential: check response.
